_comment: Animals that move. A critter is a named state machine over the tile grid, and everything about how it behaves — which states exist, what each one does, the distances it keeps and what moves it between them — is in this file. scripts/game/Critters.gd implements four goals (hold, approach, retreat, wander) and a handful of transition conditions, and knows nothing about dogs or cats. Placement is world data: an interactables record in data/world/overworld.json whose catalogue entry carries a `critter` key spawns one of these where it stands, and acting on it fires the named event. `pace` is seconds per cell, so 0.17 is exactly the player's own walk.step_time and anything larger is an amble; `critter.tick_seconds` is only how often an animal reconsiders, and is deliberately finer than any pace so a speed is never quantised to it. Numbers are here rather than in GDScript because the point of the exercise is that the next animal is a data file. The escort in #78 — "follow, but stop if the player gets too far, and fail after N tiles apart" — is three states and four transitions in this same shape and needs no new code; scripts/game/CritterSim.gd builds and runs exactly that as a proof.

critters.name: the dog
critters._comment: Follow, with lag. `trail: 2` aims him at the cell you stood on two moves ago rather than the one you are on, which is the whole difference between a companion and a mirror — a follower that occupies your previous cell exactly reads as a rendering bug. `keep: 1` means he stops when he is beside that cell, so his real distance from you sits around two or three. His pace is the player's own 0.17s a cell, so he keeps up rather than gaining or losing ground. `recover: 10` is the escape hatch: ten move attempts that get no closer and he gives up on the path and reappears at the edge of his band, which is what stops a dog wedged behind a chair from being lost for the rest of the run.

waiting.say: He sits down where he is. He will be here.

following.say: He gets up. He is coming with you.

critters.name: the cat
critters._comment: Flee, then stalk, then hold. The thresholds are deliberately different in each direction and that asymmetry is the whole design: it breaks off at 2, runs to 6, comes back in to 4 and only sets off again at 5, so the resting band is 3 to 4 and there is no distance at which two rules disagree. Matching the numbers — approach to 4, flee below 4 — would produce an animal that vibrates on the boundary, which is the failure this shape exists to avoid. `stray_gte` on the bolt is for a cat that runs out of house before it runs out of nerve: cornered, it stops and watches from wherever it got to rather than scrabbling at the wall. One asymmetry is deliberate and is the answer to a contradiction in the issue: `dozing` does NOT break on proximity. A cat that flees the moment you come within two cells is a cat with an unreachable Pet verb, because Pet needs you adjacent. So the wariness is something you teach it. Before that it only mooches -- a slow `wander` on a two-cell leash from where it was placed, which is what stops a sleeping animal from being a prop.

bolting.say: It is already three tiles away.

watching.say: It has stopped, at a distance it picked.

waiting.say: He is sitting on the step with his hands in his pockets.
